# Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of Pyridinium

# Enabled by Surface Proton Transfer Reactions

Coleman X. Kronawitter,a Γ Zhu Chen,a Peng Zhao,b Xiaofang Yang,a Bruce E. Koela*

aDepartment of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ

08544 (USA)

bDepartment of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 (USA)

ΓCurrent address: Department of Chemical Engineering, University of California, Davis,

Davis, CA 95616 (USA)

Corresponding Author

*E-mail: bkoel@princeton.edu. Tel.: 609-258-4524.

ABSTRACT. It is observed that pyridinium is hydrogenated at Pt electrodes in electrochemical

conditions consistent with those previously shown to yield selective reduction of carbon

dioxide to methanol and formic acid. The hydrogenation proceeds through a heterogeneous

reaction with chemisorbed hydrogen, which originates from one-electron surface proton

transfer reactions. After the Faradaic discharge of protons at the surface, the hydrogenation

is charge-neutral: atomic hydrogen is transferred to pyridinium, with its single electron, as

C=C(N) double bonds are reduced. Electrochemical methods are used to show that

pyridinium adsorbs on the Pt surface, consistent with the proposed heterogeneous reaction


<!-- Page 2 -->


mechanism. From this first observation of the electrochemical generation of a stable

hydrogenated piperidinium-like near-species it logically follows that dihydropyridinium, the

protonated form of the previously-proposed hydride-shuttling reduction catalyst, must

transiently exist under these conditions near the Pt surface in the presence of carbon dioxide.

Therefore partially hydrogenated heterocycles remain strong candidates for catalytically

active species that enable selective carbon dioxide reduction. More generally, the observed

mild potentials required for electrocatalytic hydrogenation of stable organics implies that

engineered transfer hydrogenations involving organic adsorbates can be a viable approach

for achieving selective carbon dioxide reduction to fuels.

TOC GRAPHICS

KEYWORDS. CO2 reduction, electrocatalysis, hydrogenation, heterocycle


<!-- Page 3 -->


TEXT. Electrocatalytic processes lie at the core of a number of emerging technologies whose

function is to drive selective fuel-forming reactions using only sunlight or renewable electricity,

water, and the constituents of air (i.e. H2O, CO2, N2, O2). Enabling these technologies requires

greater mechanistic knowledge than currently exists on the aqueous surface chemistry of organic

molecules. In the context of electrocatalytic and photoelectrocatalytic CO2 reduction to fuels, the

aqueous electrochemistry of pyridine (C5H5N; Py), a simple aromatic N-heterocycle, has been the

subject of extensive debate in a series of recent investigations.1-31 Py, or its protonated form

pyridinium (PyH+), in some way facilitates increased selectivity for desirable products, including

methanol and formic acid, in CO2-containing electrochemical cells with metal2 or semiconductor1

cathodes (a general process hereafter referred to as 'Py-catalyzed CO2 reduction' for convenience).

The details of the prior mechanistic proposals for Py-catalyzed CO2 reduction are too extensive to

provide in this short Letter, and the reader is referred to the recent literature where the debate has

been reviewed.13, 15, 18 Briefly, there are three primary narratives on the reaction mechanism in the

most current literature on Py-catalyzed CO2 reduction.  In a series of computational studies, Carter

and coworkers5-9, 13 and Keith and coworkers18 have shown that dihydropyridine (PyH2) could be

generated in the reported electrochemical conditions for CO2 reduction, and further can serve as a

shuttle for hydrides to CO2.  In the associated proposed mechanism on GaP, PyH2 forms through

a Langmuir-Hinshelwood reaction between surface-bound Py and hydridic H.6, 8, 10-11 A second

mechanism under consideration also evokes PyH2 as a hydride shuttle. The reports on this

mechanism, from Musgrave and coworkers,14-16 have emphasized that homogeneous chemical


<!-- Page 4 -->


steps must be considered for PyH2-based catalysis, and that PyH2 should be expected to regenerate

when catalyzing homogeneous CO2, HCOOH, and H2CO reduction reactions.

These mechanisms differ in many important aspects, but they share the distinct claim that Py ring

hydrogenation occurs, and that the hydricity of PyH2 is suitable to effect hydride transfer to CO2.15,

18 This contrasts starkly with the third mechanism currently under consideration,4, 12, 17, 21-22

whereby PyHaq

+  is reduced to Pyaq, resulting in adsorbed surface hydride. Next, the surface hydride

is transferred to CO2 at the electrophilic carbon and, together with the proton from another

nearby PyHaq

+ , produces HCOOH.22 The evidence now appears overwhelming that the one-

electron reduction of PyH+ at the cathode to form adsorbed hydrogen occurs on Pt group metals

under the reported conditions.  We note that differing yields for methanol have been reported in

the experimental literature dedicated to investigating the efficiency and selectivity of Py-catalyzed

CO2 reduction, including one study which failed to observe any methanol generation.3

In terms of the mechanistic investigation of this system, the essential question that remains to be

answered18 is: how do Py and/or PyH+ catalyze selective CO2 reduction to HCOOH and CH3OH

if their role is simply to serve as a Brønsted acid?  In this Letter we present evidence for a new

mechanism that reconciles conflicts among those described above, based on our observation of

electrocatalytic hydrogenation. We show experimentally that PyH+ is readily hydrogenated at Pt

cathode surfaces through heterogeneous chemical steps involving chemisorbed H (PtHads), which

need not have hydridic character.

The broad negative absorbance envelope in the spectra in Fig. 1a results from the displacement of

H2O from the thin layer of electrolyte during electrolysis (see Fig. S5-8 and associated discussion).

In the presence of Py, new spectroscopic features appear in the 3000-2700 cm-1 and 1600-1300

cm-1 energy ranges. These features coincide with vibrational modes associated with Py and

piperidine (fully hydrogenated Py, PyH6), reference spectra for which were also recorded and are

shown at the bottom of Fig 1a.

Figs. 1d,e show the spectra in Fig. 1a magnified over energy ranges characteristic of the vibrational

energies associated with CH2 stretching modes (Fig. 1d), and ring modes and CH2 bending modes

(Fig. 1e).  Figs. 1d,e also contain reference spectra obtained for PyH+ and piperidinium solutions

(50 vol%) in the same acidic electrolyte used in the electrochemical experiments. The peak

assignments in Figs. 1d,e indicate clearly that the new spectroscopic features associated the

presence of PyH+ are signatures of the consumption of PyH+ (e.g. reduction in intensity for the

PyH+ ring modes at 1490 and 1550 cm-1) and the generation of hydrogenated, piperidinium-like

species (e.g. emergent CH2 stretching modes between 3000 and 2700 cm-1 and CH2 bending modes

between 1500 and 1300 cm-1). CH stretching bands for PyH+ above 3000 cm-1 were obscured by

intense and broad OH stretching modes of displaced liquid H2O. We attribute the peak near 2500

cm-1 to the NH stretching mode associated with a cationic piperidinium complex, presumably with

electrolyte anions,32 but the discussion of this interaction is beyond the scope of this Letter. All

results are completely consistent with the increase of piperidinium bands and reduction of PyH+


<!-- Page 7 -->


bands. Using Py-d5 and D2O reveals the expected isotopic spectral shift associated with the

presence of CD2 modes (Fig. S2).

With this data, we report the first evidence for the hydrogenation of PyH+ in electrochemical

conditions consistent with those previously shown to yield selective reduction of CO2 to HCOOH

and CH3OH (see below for an elaboration on electrolyte and pH effects). Spectra associated with

hydrogenation are consistent with those of our piperidinium reference and those in the literature

for piperidinium,33 with the exception of additional intensity on the high-energy sides of the CH2

stretching bands (i.e. at 2970, 2870, and 2783 cm-1).  We can make no definitive assignment for

this blue-shifted broadening, but believe it may due to increased hydrogen bonding effects near

the electrode surface. For example, hydrogen bonding with near-surface H2O in certain

circumstances can shorten C-H bond lengths, increasing the corresponding stretching energies.34

It is also possible that there is another species present possessing sp3-hybridized C-H bonds, e.g.

amylamine resulting from Py ring opening, which would possess additional intensity in this energy

range due to CH3 groups.  However, ring opening is not observed in prior studies on gas-phase

hydrogenations of Py on Pt.35  The presence of open-chain compounds remains a possibility, but

based on the evidence currently available, we assign the new hydrogenated species to be a near-

surface H-bonded piperidinium.

In the presence of dissolved CO2, the system yields essentially identical spectra (Figs. S3,4). In

the literature, it is typically reported that methanol product exists in concentrations on the order of

1-10 ppm after electrolysis experiments.19, 30  The operando single-bounce reflectance FTIR

configuration used in this study is not sufficiently sensitive to detect such concentrations. Although


<!-- Page 8 -->


the detection limits of the system are not as yet established, as a point of reference, observation of

consumption of PyH+ through the 1490 cm-1 ring mode was only possible at initial PyH+

concentrations above about 10 mM. The present measurements do establish, however, that PyH+

hydrogenation occurs in the presence of CO2 at mild applied potentials.  Modifications to the

operando spectroscopy device are underway to increase the sensitivity of the measurements.

Observation of PyH+ hydrogenation is readily explained in the context of a class of reactions

known as electrocatalytic hydrogenations. These reactions have been studied since the early

twentieth century36 and differ from gas-phase catalytic hydrogenations in that reactive

chemisorbed H is generated by reduction of solvated protons at a cathode surface rather than

dissociative adsorption of molecular H2 at a catalyst surface.36-38 Considering the reduction of a

hydrocarbon molecule substrate Y to its dihydro-derivative YH2, electrocatalytic hydrogenation at

a metal electrode M proceeds as:

H!O" + e# + M →MH$%&+ H'O (1)

M + Y →MY$%& (2)

MY$%& + 2MH$%& →YH'. (3)

For reactions characterized by Eqs. 1-3, reduction of H!O" to form MH$%& (Eq. 1) is often the rate-

determining step.39 Note that Eq. 1 (the Volmer reaction) is a Faradaic electrochemical step and

Eq. 3 is a heterogeneous chemical step. Consequently the electrochemical current associated with

these reactions records the rate of the one-electron discharge of protons at the surface, and therefore

this mechanism is consistent with the electrochemical analysis conducted in the many prior

detailed studies on this system.3, 12, 21-22 Electrocatalytic hydrogenations (Eqs. 1-3) compete with


<!-- Page 9 -->


the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), for which MH$%& is also a reactant in the Tafel and

Heyrovsky steps.

In the context of the literature associated with Py-catalyzed CO2 reduction, it is important to note

that the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of Y to YH2 (Eqs. 1-3) is quite distinct from the charge-

equivalent electronation-protonation of Y:

Y + e# →Y•# (4)

Y•# + H" →YH• (5)

YH• + e# →YH# (6)

YH# + H" →YH'. (7)

The energetics associated with executing Eqs. 4-7 are typically much more demanding than those

of Eqs. 1-3, and Eq. 4 is commonly the potential-determining step. This required potential, E, is

given most generally by −nEF = ∆G = ∆H −T∆S, using the typical notation in electrochemical

thermodynamics. Here, ∆H is related to the energy required to place one electron in the lowest

unoccupied orbital (LUMO) of the reactant hydrocarbon,40 and a linear relationship exists between

E and the energy of the LUMO.40-41 In contrast, the rate of electrocatalytic hydrogenation of PyH+

and other organic molecules does not scale with the energies of their LUMOs. In our experiments,

we observe PyH+ hydrogenation through proton reduction at potentials as anodic as -0.35 VAg/AgCl,

which proves that the reaction does not first require the one-electron reduction of PyH+ to PtHads

(for which the potential required is -0.6 VAg/AgCl12 and is independent of pH below the pKa,21 as it

is for all weak acids).


<!-- Page 10 -->


A brief note is required on the electrolyte and the use of unbuffered solutions in much of the

literature on this subject. The data in Fig. 1 was acquired with 0.5 M H2SO4, which ostensibly

creates conditions more acidic than those used in many reports on this system. In fact the use of

this electrolyte was an intentional experimental contrivance that facilitated a high initial local

proton concentration near the Pt surface, which decreases during the reaction. We see a diffusion

overpotential for HER and observe that the adsorption kinetics of hydrogen in the underpotential

regime is quasi-reversible, in contrast to the same system unconstrained by proton diffusion (Fig.

S5). Therefore the reaction rate in the thin layer cell is controlled by both charge transfer and mass

transport of protons, and the local pH is higher during reaction than is otherwise implied by the

use of 0.5 M H2SO4.

Evidence for a local pH increase at the Pt surface comes from the simple observation that higher

cathodic potentials were required to generate current densities for proton discharge than when the

thin-layer configuration was not used.  In our experiments, a proton discharge current density of

about 1.5 mA cm-2 was required to create an observable quantity of the hydrogenated product.  If

an electrolyte with higher pH was used, PyH+ consumption could be observed, but at predictably

higher cathodic potential, completely consistent with expectations. An operando FTIR device that

provides a flow channel to facilitate the transport of protons to the electrode surface could in

principle allow greater control of the local pH of the system, although a near-surface pH gradient

with magnitude dependent on the reaction rate is inevitable.  We are in the process of building this

device for future studies.


<!-- Page 11 -->


Our results imply that in the literature on this subject,2, 22 the use of unbuffered electrolytes with

pH near 5.2 makes the one-electron reduction of PyH+ at -0.6 VAg/AgCl the dominant mechanism

for PtHads generation. However PtHads generated by H3O+ reduction and PyH+ reduction are

energetically equivalent. Our observation of PyH+ hydrogenation at very low applied cathodic

potential parallels that made in a recent investigation of product yields from pyridine-catalyzed

CO2 reduction at Pt, which reported methanol generation at applied potentials more anodic than -

0.3 VAg/AgCl.19 Given this potential, this authors of Ref [19] noted that this methanol generation

reaction must also be facilitated by Hads resulting from H3O+ reduction. The importance of these

coincident observations is discussed later in this Letter.

Electrocatalytic hydrogenations, like gas-phase hydrogenations, usually require coadsorption of

reactive Hads and the unsaturated hydrocarbon (Eq. 3). Fig. 2 provides electrochemical results

showing that PyH+ adsorbs strongly on Pt. The presence of PyH+ in the electrolyte inhibits the

adsorption and desorption of hydrogen at the Pt surface (at -0.25 to 0 VAg/AgCl) and inhibits

oxidation of the surface (above 0.6 VAg/AgCl).  This indicates the presence of an adsorbate whose

coverage can be quantified by analysis of the charge passed through the interface during hydrogen

The coverage of the adsorbate plotted with respect to bulk PyH+ solution concentration (Fig. 2b)

resembles a Langmuir isotherm.  Adsorption is not restricted to this electrolyte composition, and

adsorption was also observed in 0.5 M KCl and in a phosphate-buffered electrolyte, both with pH

5.15. Py and PyH+ adsorption will be explored further in a forthcoming publication.  Adsorption

can alternatively be observed through stripping experiments conducted in fresh electrolyte after

experiments involving aqueous Py/PyH+. Fig. 2c shows CV scans demonstrating the recovery of

the surface area of the clean Pt electrode through oxidation and/or reduction of the adsorbed

species. Regardless of the electrolyte where adsorption took place, extensive electrochemical

cycling in the fresh solution was required to recover the clean Pt surface area.

The mechanism proposed for the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of PyH+ at Pt is presented in

Scheme 1.  PyH+ adsorbs on Pt (I). After, prior to, or concurrent with this adsorption, a proton is

discharged at the Pt surface in a Faradaic, one-electron electrochemical step, forming chemisorbed

PtHads (II).  The hydrogen can originate from either H3O+ or PyH+, depending on potential and pH.

Finally, in heterogeneous chemical steps, PyH+ is fully hydrogenated by PtHads in Langmuir-

Hinshelwood reactions, with ortho- or para-dihydropyridinium as an intermediate on or near the

surface (III). This reaction mechanism is analogous to the majority of prior proposals for

electrocatalytic hydrogenations and should be uncontroversial.36 The rate of reaction is expected

to be highest at electrodes associated with rapid H+ adsorption kinetics (e.g. Pt, Ir, Rh, and Pd).


<!-- Page 14 -->


Scheme 1. Proposed reaction mechanism for electrocatalytic hydrogenation of PyH+.

To confirm the validity of this mechanism we studied the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of

benzene, which possesses no labile proton, under identical conditions. Fig. 3 shows operando

FTIR spectra recorded in the presence of benzene. The new sp3-hybridized C-H stretching bands

at 2927 and 2853 cm-1 are a signature of cyclohexane,42 indicating complete hydrogenation. This

result confirms our mechanistic claim because the electronation of benzene (Eq. 4) occurs only at

-3.4 VSCE at Pt electrodes,43 due to the high-lying LUMO of benzene.  In stark contrast, we observe

benzene hydrogenation to cyclohexane at as anodic as -0.40 VSCE. In fact, benzene is known to be

hydrogenated at even more anodic potentials, i.e. using only underpotential-deposited hydrogen.44

The mechanistic claim made here for PyH+ should not be considered controversial ̶ the literature

associated with electrocatalytic hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons is vast, spans several

decades, and includes demonstrations of hydrogenations of a great diversity of aromatics and

alkenes.  Examples from the literature of electrocatalytic hydrogenations at Pt reported with mild

applied potentials of about 0 ± 0.2 VRHE include (with associated saturated products): ethylene

(ethane),45 propene (propane),46 benzene (cyclohexane),47 toluene (methylcyclohexane),48 1,4-

hydroquinone (1,4 cyclohexanediol),49 1,2,4-benzenetriol (1,2,4-cyclohexanetriol),49 4-

aminophenol (4-aminocyclohexanol),49 and 1,4-dihydroxy-naphthalene (1,4-dihydroxy-

decahydro-naphthalene).49 The hydrogenation of many other organic molecules, including


<!-- Page 16 -->


numerous polyaromatics, has been reported through galvanostatic experiments and with other

electrode materials.36 The results presented here are fully consistent with those described in this

extensive literature.  Given these examples, Py is also expected to be hydrogenated if an adequate

surface density of coadsorbed Hads is established. Near the pKa, Hads can be generated by PyH+

reduction.  Additionally, although here we refer to the molecular substrate as PyH+, evidence exists

showing that in acidic conditions Py adsorbs on Pt because the strong interaction between N and

Pt prevents protonation near the surface.50

This first observation of the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of pyridinium to a piperidinium-like

species through surface-adsorbed hydrogen leads to the logical conclusion that dihydropyridinium,

the protonated form of the partially hydrogenated species previously proposed to be the active

catalyst for CO2 reduction, must transiently exist on or very near the polarized electrode surface.

This conclusion follows from the observed near-universality of the stepwise addition mechanism

in heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation reactions.51  That dihydropyridine could exist as a

transient intermediate has been proposed in a recent theoretical analysis of this system.18 Our

observation of piperidinium generation suggests that in order for a transient dihydropyridinium

species to be an efficient catalyst, the system must be designed such that the rate of reaction with

CO2 is faster than the rate of reaction with surface PtHads, which leads to further hydrogenation.

Furthermore, our observation of pyridinium hydrogenation in the presence of dissolved CO2

requires that dihydropyridinium transiently co-exists with CO2 near the electrode surface, and our

findings therefore provide direct experimental evidence for the relevance of many prior theoretical

treatments of CO2 reduction catalysis by dihydropyridine.6, 8, 14-15 We note that the generation of

piperidinium in our experiment implies that much of the pyridine present near the surface is


<!-- Page 17 -->


consumed, and therefore future experiments designed to optimize CO2 reduction efficiency should

emphasize the importance of catalyst regeneration.

The observations made here can be further interpreted in the context of conclusions from a recent

investigation of the CO2 pressure dependence of pyridine-catalyzed CO2 reduction at a Pt

cathode.19  In that study it was determined that the generation of methanol is a transient process

that is decoupled from interfacial charge transfer. Similarly, in this Letter, we report that the

hydrogenation of PyH+ is a chemical step that is facilitated by, but decoupled from, the Faradaic

discharge of protons at the surface. Therefore, taken together with results in Ref [19], the new

experimental evidence indicates that both PyH+ and CO2 are hydrogenated through heterogeneous

chemical reactions that follow from simple electrochemical surface proton transfer reactions.

Whether the associated hydrogen source is PyH+ or H3O+ depends on system properties including

pH and polarization potential. Although at present our measurements are not sufficiently sensitive

to probe a surface reaction between CO2 and hydrogenated PyH+, a wealth of information exists

in the literature regarding the favorable thermodynamics of this interaction.6, 8, 14-15, 23  Going

forward, surface-sensitive, time-resolved, operando infrared spectroscopies are expected to be

most suitable for examining the transient and rate-limiting aspects of hydrogen transfers to both

CO2 and N-containing heteroaromatic catalysts.

In light of these results, partially hydrogenated heterocycles must remain strong candidates for

active, hydrogen-shuttling species in CO2 reduction catalysis.  More generally, the mild applied

potentials (near 0 VRHE) required for electrocatalytic hydrogenation of organic molecules provides


<!-- Page 18 -->


an approach for engineered transfer hydrogenations involving organic adsorbates, which can be a

viable tool for the design of selective CO2 reduction systems.
